newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek government takes tough line with farmers.
newsitem.headline: Greek government takes tough line with farmers.

text.p: Greece's socialist government took a tough line on Wednesday with farmers who have blockaded road and rail links for seven days, saying it had no new offers and the protesters should free the nation's highways.
"The positions of the government are known. We have nothing new to propose (to the farmers)," Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas told reporters after a special cabinet meeting.
"Those who have erected blockades should ... remove them and free the roads," he said, stopping short of saying what would be done if the defiant farmers refused.

He said he would take the government's stand to the farmers later on Wednesday, visiting government prefects and farmers' representatives in their headquarters in the western mainland town of Larissa.
The government's stand looks set to plunge Greece further into crisis, with farmers telling television reporters at the barricades that the minister's comments were unacceptable.
"We are asking only for our just rights. If we get them, we will leave immediately. If we don't, we'll stay until Christmas and beyond," one Larissa farmer told Star television channel.
A ragtag army of more than 10,000 colourful tractors has fanned out across Greece, seizing toll booths and blockading national road and rail links at more than 40 points.
Sprawling tent cities line major roads, with tables, chairs, food and drink. Groups of farmers sit around bonfires for warmth.
Border roads to Bulgaria and Turkey have been blocked, stopping all traffic. The entrance to Salonika international airport, Greece's second city and main northern port, is cut.

Passengers headed for Salonika airport stop at the farmers' barricade and trudge 200 metres (yards) to the other side where, usually, a bus meets them. But many passengers have missed the bus and had to walk through the wind and rain to the terminal.
The blockade began last Thursday and has left hundreds of international and domestic lorries stranded. Drivers have been complaining about lack of food, water and sanitation.
Food merchants said stocks remain high, and prices largely under control, but have warned customers that should the protest continue next week there will be real problems.
"Of course the prices will go up. Where are we going to get meat from? They will have to go up," butcher Paulos Zachos told Reuters Television at the central Athens meat market.
Concern among customers was growing, too, and there were signs of stockpiling in anticipation of a long protest ahead.
"I shopped enough for a week because I don't know how long this will continue and we have to be prepared," said Pandelis Papadopoulos, who was weighted down with supplies.
Farmers had expected Prime Minister Costas Simitis, who chaired Wednesday's cabinet meeting, to make new proposals but he was in no mood for compromise.
Simitis, who won September elections, is facing the toughest challenge so far to his economic plans, which give priority to meeting European Union convergence targets.
The blockade has caused transport chaos throughout Greece but farmers have vowed to continue to press demands for better prices, cheaper fuel and rescheduling $1.3 billion in debts.
Simitis stripped away many tax exemptions last week when he submitted his 1997 austerity budget and is facing opposition from other groups as well.

Pensioners, housewives, teachers, tax and port officials, and the civil servants union have all called strikes. Dockers have been on strike for a week over pension rights, and cargo has gone unloaded.
